newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt says Israeli leaders talking like "dinosaurs".
newsitem.headline: Egypt says Israeli leaders talking like "dinosaurs".

text.p: An Egyptian official said on Monday Israeli leaders were talking like "dinosaurs" about the situation in the Middle East and were amateur politicians.
"The language used by Israeli officials is the language of dinosaurs, it goes against the logic of this age," assistant foreign minister Fathi el-Shazli told reporters.
"This language provokes disgust because Israel is a party to what is called the peace process and it has obligations towards various other parties," he added.

Shazli was referring to an interview Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu gave the German Der Spiegel magazine in which he said there would never be a Palestinian state, and to warnings Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai levelled at Syria over its troop movements in Lebanon.
Netanyahu came to power in May on a platform that rejected the creation of a Palestinian state and promised a tougher line with Arab peace partners.

"This banging of war drums by Israeli officials and the threat to resort to the military option will not help create the necessary groundwork for the success of any peace efforts because it will doubtless create equal reactions," Shazli said.

"It also affirms what I have said before, as an Arab citizen, that the Israeli government includes amateur politicians who are unaware of the responsibilities of a government which is a member of the world community," he added.
Shazli said Israel could never be a dominant force in the region because of the historical baggage it carries.

"Israel is just a limited market. It lacks the demographic and human resources and its cultural influence is non-existent. It has a historical role which can only be seen as negative in every way. It brings to mind bad memories at the regional level, vicious mental images," he added.
Shazli's comments were among the strongest in a war of words brewing since Netanyahu won elections in May.
Egypt in 1979 became the first Arab country to sign a peace treaty with Israel but relations between the two countries over the years have often been strained.
